To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) long-range dependence in the traffic on a link depends on the time of day and day of week; 2) long-range dependence depends on the year in which data are collected, even when traffic is measured in terms of bytes, not packets; 3) long-range dependence is affected by the presence and absence of a single UDP application; and 4) the Hurst parameter is not the only measure of long-range dependence.

(i) there are large differences in the long-range dependent characteristics of Internet traffic between 2002 and early 2003, (ii) these differences are driven by a single application, and (iii) these differences do not show up in the byte counts.

(a) there is a single UDP application whose presence or absence in 2002 and in 2003, respectively, is the main cause for the observed large differences in traffic characteristics, (b) the differences are not reflected in the byte counts, and (c) the differences in the packet count are not due to differences in packet sizes.

a detailed study of long-range dependence (LRD) in Internet traffic, with a particular emphasis on the effects of time-of-day, time-of-year, day-of-week and protocol variations on the LRD properties of the traffic.

the following issues: (1) the impact of long-range dependence on the performance of Internet applications, and (2) the impact of non-stationarity on the performance of long-range dependence estimators.

the Internet is a complex and dynamic system whose behavior is not well understood.
the long-range dependence of Internet traffic has changed significantly over the last few years, and the changes have been driven by the evolution of the Internet itself.
Internet traffic is not only non-stationary in time, but also in space.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Internet traffic mix is continually evolving, which has significant implications for network engineering and traffic modeling.
the Internet traffic is not stationary, and that long-range dependence is not universal in Internet traffic.
long-range dependence is a robust property in Internet traffic, but the exact values of the Hurst parameter are not.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Internet traffic is continually changing and that the changes can be large enough to invalidate the results of previous studies.
the traffic mix on an Internet link is continually evolving, and that the traffic statistics can vary significantly between years.
long-range dependence in Internet traffic is not a constant property, but can vary significantly over time.
